abstract: This lecture covers cardiovascular risk reduction, a core primary care topic. It emphasizes that heart disease is the leading cause of death in the US and that half of all heart attacks are caused by five modifiable risk factors: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. The talk focuses on lipid screening guidelines, statin therapy as the cornerstone of risk reduction, and the use of the ASCVD risk calculator to guide treatment decisions. Key teaching points include when to screen for familial hypercholesterolemia, how to monitor statin therapy, and how to manage common side effects like myalgias.
key_points: Half of all heart attacks are caused by five modifiable risk factors: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes.
USPSTF recommends lipid screening starting at age 11 for familial hypercholesterolemia, then every 5 years from age 40 to 75 for those without risk factors.
Non-fasting lipid panels are acceptable unless triglycerides are over 400, which requires a fasting sample to calculate LDL.
The Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria can diagnose familial hypercholesterolemia with a score >8, even without genetic testing.
ASCVD risk score <10%: lifestyle modifications; 10-20%: moderate-dose statin; >20%: high-dose statin.
After starting a statin, recheck lipids at 6-12 weeks, then annually; routine monitoring of LFTs and CK is not indicated.
Statins reduce LDL by 30-50% depending on dose; atorvastatin 10 mg gives ~30% reduction, 20 mg gives ~45% reduction.
Common statin side effects include myalgias (7-20%), elevated LFTs, and a small increase in diabetes risk, but cardiovascular benefits far outweigh these risks.
For statin-associated myalgias, options include switching to a less intense statin (e.g., pravastatin), reducing dose, or using every-other-day dosing.
